question.text: What does a stop sign at a railroad crossing require when no train is in sight?

answer.text: A stop sign at a railroad crossing means you must stop even when no train is visible.

teaching.text: A crossing stop sign is a full stop every time, train or no train. Remember: stop sign means stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A stop sign at a railroad crossing means you must stop even when no train is visible.

question.text: Which vehicles must stop at a crossing even with no stop sign or signal?

answer.text: Unless signs say otherwise, school buses, for-hire passenger vehicles, gasoline trucks and other vehicles hauling hazardous materials must stop and confirm no train is coming even without a stop sign or signal.

teaching.text: Passengers and dangerous loads mean these vehicles stop at every crossing. Remember: buses, hire vehicles, hazmat stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Unless signs say otherwise, school buses, for-hire passenger vehicles, gasoline trucks and other vehicles hauling hazardous materials must stop and confirm no train is coming even without a stop sign or signal.

question.text: What is a passive railroad crossing?

answer.text: Passive crossings have no flashing lights or gates; they rely on advance warning signs, pavement markings and crossbucks with yield or stop signs at or just before the tracks.

teaching.text: No device will warn you at a passive crossing, so the checking is yours. Remember: passive: signs and markings only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passive crossings have no flashing lights or gates; they rely on advance warning signs, pavement markings and crossbucks with yield or stop signs at or just before the tracks.

question.text: How do you cross at a passive crossing?

answer.text: At a passive crossing, slow or stop as needed, yield to trains, check both directions, make sure every track is clear, and never race a train.

teaching.text: Every track must be clear, because one train can hide another. Remember: yield, look, never race.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a passive crossing, slow or stop as needed, yield to trains, check both directions, make sure every track is clear, and never race a train.

question.text: How does an active crossing warn of a train?

answer.text: Active crossings warn of a train with some mix of gates, flashing lights, message signs, and bells or other sounds.

teaching.text: When an active crossing's devices start, a train is on its way. Remember: active: gates, lights, bells.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Active crossings warn of a train with some mix of gates, flashing lights, message signs, and bells or other sounds.

question.text: How do passive and active crossings differ?

answer.text: Passive crossings use signs and markings only, while active crossings add gates, flashing lights or bells that announce a train.

teaching.text: Passive means you do the warning work yourself. Remember: signs only versus signals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passive crossings use signs and markings only, while active crossings add gates, flashing lights or bells that announce a train.

question.text: When must you stop at an active crossing?

answer.text: Stop whenever crossing bells ring, lights flash, or the gate is down or moving, and never drive through, around or under an activated crossing.

teaching.text: A moving gate already means stop, and going around it is never allowed. Remember: bells or lights: stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stop whenever crossing bells ring, lights flash, or the gate is down or moving, and never drive through, around or under an activated crossing.

question.text: After a train passes, when may you cross?

answer.text: After a train passes, wait until the gates rise, lights and bells stop, and you are sure all tracks are clear.

teaching.text: A second train can follow the first, so wait for the gates, the signals and a clear view. Remember: wait for all clear.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After a train passes, wait until the gates rise, lights and bells stop, and you are sure all tracks are clear.

question.text: What habits keep you safe while crossing tracks?

answer.text: Never stop on tracks, always expect a train, look both ways, and avoid changing gears while crossing.

teaching.text: Commit to a steady crossing with no stops and no gear changes. Remember: never stop on tracks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never stop on tracks, always expect a train, look both ways, and avoid changing gears while crossing.

question.text: How should you cross tracks on a snowy road?

answer.text: On a snowy road, cross tracks with enough speed that you will not get stuck.

teaching.text: Snow around rails can hold a slow car, so keep enough momentum. Remember: keep momentum on snow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a snowy road, cross tracks with enough speed that you will not get stuck.

question.text: When traffic is backed up past a crossing, when may you start across?

answer.text: When traffic may be backed up near a crossing, do not start across unless your vehicle can clear the far side of the tracks by at least six feet.

teaching.text: Look past the crossing first and make sure your whole car fits on the far side. Remember: room to clear first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When traffic may be backed up near a crossing, do not start across unless your vehicle can clear the far side of the tracks by at least six feet.

question.text: How much warning do you get once crossing signals start?

answer.text: Once crossing lights and gates activate or you hear a train horn, you have about twenty seconds before the train arrives.

teaching.text: Twenty seconds is the train's warning, not your chance to cross. Remember: about twenty seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Once crossing lights and gates activate or you hear a train horn, you have about twenty seconds before the train arrives.

question.text: What clearance and warning time apply at a busy crossing?

answer.text: You must clear the far side of the tracks by six feet before crossing into backed-up traffic, and you get only about twenty seconds of warning once the signals start.

teaching.text: Six goes with distance in feet; twenty goes with time in seconds. Remember: six feet, twenty seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You must clear the far side of the tracks by six feet before crossing into backed-up traffic, and you get only about twenty seconds of warning once the signals start.

question.text: You are stuck on the tracks and a train is coming. What do you do?

answer.text: If you are stuck on the tracks and the gates are activated or a train is clearly coming, get everyone out and far from the tracks right away, then call nine one one.

teaching.text: With a train coming, people leave first and the call comes after. Remember: get out, then call.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you are stuck on the tracks and the gates are activated or a train is clearly coming, get everyone out and far from the tracks right away, then call nine one one.

question.text: You are stuck on the tracks with no train or signals. What do you do?

answer.text: If stuck with no activated lights or gates and no train in sight, get everyone out and away, then call the railroad's number on the blue Emergency Notification Sign and report the crossing ID.

teaching.text: With time to spare, the railroad can stop the train once you report the crossing. Remember: out, then call railroad.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If stuck with no activated lights or gates and no train in sight, get everyone out and away, then call the railroad's number on the blue Emergency Notification Sign and report the crossing ID.

question.text: What is on the crossing ID, and what can railroad officials do?

answer.text: The crossing ID on the Emergency Notification Sign has six digits and one letter; railroad officials may slow, stop or divert a train, and you then call nine one one.

teaching.text: Reading the crossing ID tells railroad officials exactly where to slow, stop or divert trains. Remember: report the crossing ID.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The crossing ID on the Emergency Notification Sign has six digits and one letter; railroad officials may slow, stop or divert a train, and you then call nine one one.

question.text: What does an Emergency Notification System sign give you?

answer.text: An Emergency Notification System sign at or near a grade crossing gives a phone number and the crossing's US DOT number for reporting emergencies or broken warning devices.

teaching.text: The blue sign is your direct line to the railroad for emergencies and broken devices. Remember: blue sign, phone number.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: An Emergency Notification System sign at or near a grade crossing gives a phone number and the crossing's US DOT number for reporting emergencies or broken warning devices.

question.text: When stuck on tracks, when do you call emergency services and when the railroad?

answer.text: If stuck on tracks with a train coming or gates down, get out and call nine one one; if no train is in sight and nothing is activated, get everyone out and call the railroad emergency number on the blue sign.

teaching.text: Getting out always comes first; the train or signals decide the call. Remember: train coming: emergency first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If stuck on tracks with a train coming or gates down, get out and call nine one one; if no train is in sight and nothing is activated, get everyone out and call the railroad emergency number on the blue sign.

question.text: What should you do every time you park?

answer.text: Whenever you park, turn off the engine, set the parking brake rather than trusting the transmission, take the keys and lock the vehicle.

teaching.text: Make the same four steps every time you park. Remember: engine off, brake, lock.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Whenever you park, turn off the engine, set the parking brake rather than trusting the transmission, take the keys and lock the vehicle.

question.text: What should you check before opening your door?

answer.text: Before opening your door, watch for passing bicycles, motorcycles, mopeds and vehicles and check your mirrors.

teaching.text: A door opened into a cyclist's path can throw the rider into traffic. Remember: look before you open.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before opening your door, watch for passing bicycles, motorcycles, mopeds and vehicles and check your mirrors.

question.text: Why open the driver's door with your right hand?

answer.text: Opening the driver's door with your right hand turns you to look over your left shoulder for oncoming cyclists and pedestrians.

teaching.text: Reaching across with the far hand turns your head toward what is coming. Remember: far hand turns your head.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Opening the driver's door with your right hand turns you to look over your left shoulder for oncoming cyclists and pedestrians.

question.text: Which way should you face walking back to the driver's side?

answer.text: Walk back to the driver's side facing oncoming traffic.

teaching.text: Facing traffic lets you see a car drifting toward you. Remember: face oncoming traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Walk back to the driver's side facing oncoming traffic.

question.text: Which way do you turn your wheels parking on a hill?

answer.text: Parking downhill, turn the wheels toward the curb; parking uphill, turn them away from the curb; with no curb, turn them so the vehicle will not roll into traffic.

teaching.text: Turned wheels let the curb catch a rolling car instead of the lane. Remember: downhill toward, uphill away.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parking downhill, turn the wheels toward the curb; parking uphill, turn them away from the curb; with no curb, turn them so the vehicle will not roll into traffic.

question.text: Why set the parking brake on a hill?

answer.text: Always set the parking brake on a hill, because the transmission is not built to act as a brake.

teaching.text: The parking brake holds the car; turned wheels are only the backup. Remember: transmission is not a brake.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always set the parking brake on a hill, because the transmission is not built to act as a brake.

question.text: How do wheel positions differ for downhill and uphill parking?

answer.text: Wheels turn toward the curb when parked downhill and away from the curb when parked uphill.

teaching.text: Picture the car rolling, and point the wheels so the curb stops it. Remember: down toward, up away.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Wheels turn toward the curb when parked downhill and away from the curb when parked uphill.

question.text: How do you start a parallel park?

answer.text: To parallel park, choose a space on the passenger side, signal, check mirrors, and pull alongside the car ahead of the space leaving two to five feet between you.

teaching.text: Feet of space beside the car ahead give your rear room to swing in. Remember: pull alongside the car ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To parallel park, choose a space on the passenger side, signal, check mirrors, and pull alongside the car ahead of the space leaving two to five feet between you.

question.text: How do you begin backing into a parallel space?

answer.text: Brake, shift to reverse, check traffic behind, then back slowly while checking mirrors and looking over your right shoulder.

teaching.text: Back slowly and look toward the space over your right shoulder. Remember: reverse, look right, go slow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Brake, shift to reverse, check traffic behind, then back slowly while checking mirrors and looking over your right shoulder.

question.text: How do you steer while backing into a parallel space?

answer.text: Turn the wheel right as you start backing to angle the rear in, then turn the other way once the rear is mostly in, making an S turn that straightens the car.

teaching.text: Two opposite turns trace an S and straighten the car. Remember: right, then left: S turn.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turn the wheel right as you start backing to angle the rear in, then turn the other way once the rear is mostly in, making an S turn that straightens the car.

question.text: How do you finish a parallel park?

answer.text: Center the car in the space, park no more than six to twelve inches from the curb, and check traffic before opening your door.

teaching.text: Inches from the curb keeps the car out of the lane. Remember: center it, close to curb.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Center the car in the space, park no more than six to twelve inches from the curb, and check traffic before opening your door.

question.text: What are the two distances in a parallel park?

answer.text: When parallel parking, pull up two to five feet beside the car ahead, and finish no more than six to twelve inches from the curb.

teaching.text: Feet first beside the car, inches last from the curb. Remember: two to five, then close.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When parallel parking, pull up two to five feet beside the car ahead, and finish no more than six to twelve inches from the curb.

question.text: Can someone without a cane or wheelchair be entitled to a disability space?

answer.text: Disabilities are not always visible, so someone without a cane or wheelchair may still be entitled to a disability space.

teaching.text: Judge the placard, not the person's appearance. Remember: not all disabilities show.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Disabilities are not always visible, so someone without a cane or wheelchair may still be entitled to a disability space.

question.text: What gives free parking to a vehicle with a disability placard?

answer.text: Free parking is given only to vehicles showing a disability placard with a yellow free-parking sticker, which has stricter rules than a disability plate or placard.

teaching.text: Free parking needs the yellow sticker, which carries stricter rules. Remember: yellow sticker, free parking.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Free parking is given only to vehicles showing a disability placard with a yellow free-parking sticker, which has stricter rules than a disability plate or placard.

question.text: Who may use a disability parking space?

answer.text: To use a disability space, you or your passenger must have a qualifying disability, such as blindness or a temporary or permanent condition that greatly limits walking or needs an assistive device, plus a disability plate or placard.

teaching.text: The space needs both a qualifying person and a plate or placard. Remember: qualifying disability plus placard.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To use a disability space, you or your passenger must have a qualifying disability, such as blindness or a temporary or permanent condition that greatly limits walking or needs an assistive device, plus a disability plate or placard.

question.text: When should you not use a disability space even with a placard?

answer.text: Do not use a disability space if no occupant is disabled or the disabled person is not going into the store with you.

teaching.text: The placard belongs to the person, so the person must be going in. Remember: no disabled rider, no space.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not use a disability space if no occupant is disabled or the disabled person is not going into the store with you.

question.text: Why must you keep off the striped area of a van-accessible space?

answer.text: Van-accessible spaces are wider to fit a wheelchair lift and ramp, so never park on their blue-striped area or block ramps and curb cuts.

teaching.text: The striped area is room for a lift or ramp, not extra parking. Remember: stripes are for ramps.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Van-accessible spaces are wider to fit a wheelchair lift and ramp, so never park on their blue-striped area or block ramps and curb cuts.

question.text: What does a disability plate or placard allow, and what does the yellow sticker add?

answer.text: A disability plate or placard lets you use a disability space, but only a placard with the yellow sticker gives free parking.

teaching.text: The plate or placard answers where you park; the sticker answers whether you pay. Remember: placard parks, sticker frees.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A disability plate or placard lets you use a disability space, but only a placard with the yellow sticker gives free parking.

question.text: Can local parking rules be stricter than state law?

answer.text: Local parking ordinances may be stricter than state law, with signs posted at city limits.

teaching.text: State rules are a floor; a city can set tighter ones. Remember: city rules can be stricter.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Local parking ordinances may be stricter than state law, with signs posted at city limits.

question.text: Who pays a ticket for an illegally parked vehicle?

answer.text: The owner of an illegally parked vehicle pays the ticket, or the person leasing it if the vehicle is leased.

teaching.text: The ticket follows the vehicle to its owner or lessee. Remember: owner or lessee pays.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The owner of an illegally parked vehicle pays the ticket, or the person leasing it if the vehicle is leased.

question.text: Where do posted signs or emergencies forbid parking?

answer.text: Never park where no stopping, no standing or no parking signs are posted, or within five hundred feet of a fire or crash.

teaching.text: Posted bans and emergency scenes keep crews and traffic moving. Remember: signs and fires: no parking.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never park where no stopping, no standing or no parking signs are posted, or within five hundred feet of a fire or crash.

question.text: Which doorways and views must you never block when parking?

answer.text: Do not park in front of a driveway, alley, theater, emergency exit or fire escape, or where you block the view of drivers turning at an intersection.

teaching.text: Never stand your car between people and their way out, or between a driver and the view. Remember: keep exits and views open.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not park in front of a driveway, alley, theater, emergency exit or fire escape, or where you block the view of drivers turning at an intersection.

question.text: How far from the curb, and facing which way, may you park?

answer.text: Never park more than twelve inches from the curb or facing against traffic.

teaching.text: Close to the curb and facing the same way as traffic is the only legal position. Remember: close to curb, with traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never park more than twelve inches from the curb or facing against traffic.

question.text: Where on bridges, tunnels and highways may you not park?

answer.text: Do not park on or under a bridge unless posted, on an overpass or in a tunnel, and outside city or village limits do not park in a highway lane when there is a shoulder.

teaching.text: Bridges, overpasses and tunnels leave no room to get around a parked car. Remember: no bridges, tunnels, highway lanes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not park on or under a bridge unless posted, on an overpass or in a tunnel, and outside city or village limits do not park in a highway lane when there is a shoulder.

question.text: Which walkways and lanes must you never park on?

answer.text: Do not park on a sidewalk, in front of a public or private driveway, or inside an intersection, crosswalk or marked bike lane.

teaching.text: Walkways and bike lanes belong to people walking and riding. Remember: off sidewalks and bike lanes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not park on a sidewalk, in front of a public or private driveway, or inside an intersection, crosswalk or marked bike lane.

question.text: Which other parking acts are illegal?

answer.text: Double parking beside a legally parked vehicle, blocking a rural mailbox, and parking at a transit stop are all illegal.

teaching.text: Double parking blocks a lane, and transit stops and mailboxes must stay reachable. Remember: no double parking.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Double parking beside a legally parked vehicle, blocking a rural mailbox, and parking at a transit stop are all illegal.

question.text: Who receives a parking ticket for a leased car?

answer.text: A parking ticket goes to the vehicle's owner, or to the person leasing it if the vehicle is leased, not simply to whoever parked it.

teaching.text: Focus on who owns or leases the car, not who parked it. Remember: the lessee pays.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A parking ticket goes to the vehicle's owner, or to the person leasing it if the vehicle is leased, not simply to whoever parked it.

question.text: How far must you park from a fire hydrant?

answer.text: Never park within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant.

teaching.text: Firefighters need room to reach a hydrant. Remember: fifteen from a hydrant.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never park within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant.

question.text: How far must you park from a fire station driveway?

answer.text: Keep twenty feet from a fire station driveway on your side of the street, and seventy-five feet from it on the opposite side when marked.

teaching.text: Fire trucks swing wide, so the far side of the street needs more room when marked. Remember: twenty here, seventy-five across.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep twenty feet from a fire station driveway on your side of the street, and seventy-five feet from it on the opposite side when marked.

question.text: How far must you park from a railroad crossing?

answer.text: Never park within fifty feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing.

teaching.text: The railroad sits at the top of the distance ladder. Remember: fifty from the rail.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never park within fifty feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing.

question.text: How far must you park from a stop sign or traffic light?

answer.text: Keep at least thirty feet away from a stop sign, traffic light or flashing beacon when parking, and the same applies to a warning sign.

teaching.text: Parked cars can hide signs, so give them room. Remember: thirty from signs and signals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep at least thirty feet away from a stop sign, traffic light or flashing beacon when parking, and the same applies to a warning sign.

question.text: How far must you park from a crosswalk or a plain intersection?

answer.text: Stay twenty feet from a marked crosswalk, or fifteen feet from an intersection that has no crosswalk.

teaching.text: Marked crosswalks get more room than plain corners. Remember: twenty crosswalk, fifteen corner.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stay twenty feet from a marked crosswalk, or fifteen feet from an intersection that has no crosswalk.

question.text: Which parking distance goes with a hydrant, a fire station driveway, a stop sign and a rail?

answer.text: Parking distances differ by object: fifteen feet from a hydrant, twenty feet from a fire station driveway on your side, thirty feet from a stop sign or signal, and fifty feet from the nearest rail.

teaching.text: Match the object to its rung: hydrant, station, signs, rail. Remember: fifteen, twenty, thirty, fifty.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parking distances differ by object: fifteen feet from a hydrant, twenty feet from a fire station driveway on your side, thirty feet from a stop sign or signal, and fifty feet from the nearest rail.

question.text: How does the fire station driveway distance change across the street?

answer.text: A fire station driveway needs twenty feet of clearance on the same side of the street but seventy-five feet on the opposite side when that distance is marked.

teaching.text: Same side twenty, opposite side seventy-five when marked. Remember: twenty same, seventy-five opposite.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A fire station driveway needs twenty feet of clearance on the same side of the street but seventy-five feet on the opposite side when that distance is marked.

question.text: How do the crosswalk and plain-intersection distances differ?

answer.text: Parking near a crosswalk requires twenty feet, but near an intersection without a crosswalk the gap is fifteen feet.

teaching.text: Ask first whether the corner has a marked crosswalk. Remember: crosswalk twenty, corner fifteen.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Parking near a crosswalk requires twenty feet, but near an intersection without a crosswalk the gap is fifteen feet.
